source: Cl. 5.1.2: explosives and detonators must be transported separately and not in the same vehicle; no explosive in the driver's cab.

q: What is the maximum number of charges that should be prepared and loaded for any single firing operation?
source: Cl. 5.1.3.1: a maximum of ten charges should be prepared and loaded for any single firing operation; count the shots fired.

q: A Controlling Team wants to start work in a new desert area. Which form of EOD clearance is acceptable under KOC.SA.025?
options: Verbal confirmation from the EOD contractor's supervisor
A printed EOD certificate with the cleared area marked on a map
An e-mail from any HSE Officer stating the area is clear
A note on the Permit to Work that the area appears clear
source: Cl. 5.2.3: EOD certification shall be issued on printed format with extent of clearance marked on a map; verbal clearance is not acceptable.

q: An electrically fired charge has misfired. What is the minimum waiting time before anyone approaches it?
source: Cl. 5.1.3.2: not less than 10 minutes for firing by electricity (30 minutes for safety fuse).

q: At what minimum distance from the explosive store building or containers must the security fence be located?
source: Cl. 5.1.1.1: explosive storage facility shall be enclosed by fencing at least 15 m from the building or containers.

q: How far from the walls must the wooden shelves holding explosive boxes be placed?
source: Cl. 5.1.1.2: boxes stacked on wooden shelves placed at least 15 cm (6") away from walls for air circulation.

q: Within what distance of a box of explosives is it prohibited to carry a lighter, matches or mobile phone?
source: Cl. 5.1.3.1: prohibited to carry lighter, matches, mobile phone or any ignition source within 30 m (100 ft) of explosives.

q: Who may travel in a vehicle carrying explosives?
options: Any crew members going to the site
The driver and one trained attendant
The driver only, with no attendant
Up to four trained shot firers
source: Cl. 5.1.2.2: the driver shall be accompanied by one trained attendant; no extra person is permitted.

q: When must a vehicle carrying explosives be refuelled?
options: When the tank falls below one quarter
Only on highways with police escort
At any fuel station on the way
source: Cl. 5.1.2.2: sufficient fuel before loading, as refuelling is not permitted during transportation.

q: What hand lamps must a vehicle carrying explosives carry?
options: Two IS lamps, one red glass, one clear
No lamps; hazard lights are enough
Two LED lamps of any colour
One ordinary torch with spare batteries
source: Cl. 5.1.2.2: two battery operated intrinsically safe hand lamps, one fitted with red glass and the other clear.

q: Detonators and high explosives with a mass explosion risk and minor missile effect belong to which category?
source: Cl. 2.0: Category ZZ — mass explosion risk and minor missile effect, e.g. high explosives, detonators, detonating fuse.

q: How often must the Controlling Team inspect each explosive storage facility?
source: Cl. 4.3 / 5.1.1.4: inspect explosive storage facilities at least every three months.

q: If tamping is needed after a cartridge is placed in a shot hole, what rod must be used?
options: A steel bar of suitable length
A wooden rod with no ferrous parts
source: Cl. 5.1.3.1: in case of tamping need, a wooden rod without any ferrous part is to be used.

q: Unused or loose explosives returned to store should be consumed or disposed of within:
source: Cl. 5.1.4: unutilized or loose explosive materials should be consumed or disposed of within one week of return.

q: How must detonator leads be kept while in storage?
options: Taped firmly to the explosive cartridges
Connected to the exploder unit in store
Shunted together until just before use
source: Cl. 5.1.1.3: detonator leads must be shunted together while stored and kept this way until right before use.

q: What material must a portable container for carrying explosives be made of?
options: Any metal box with a tight lid
Mild steel box with a padlock
source: Cl. 5.1.2.1: container and cover must be of non-ferrous material (leather, rubber, plastic, wood, canvas); fittings of brass.

q: What is the minimum distance from a hydrocarbon-carrying pipeline within which mechanical excavation (including levelling with an excavator) is prohibited?
source: Cl. 5.4 b): no mechanical excavation closer than 5 m to any hydrocarbon carrying pipeline, even for levelling.

q: Without a Management of Change and risk assessment, mechanical excavation should not take place closer than what distance to non-hydrocarbon pipelines, cables and services?
source: Cl. 5.4 c): no mechanical excavation closer than 3 m to non-hydrocarbon pipelines, cables and services; MOC and risk assessment if closer.

q: In a trench deeper than 1 m, how must access ladders be provided under KOC.SA.026?
options: Projecting 0.5 m above the edge, every 15 m of travel
Projecting 1 m above the edge, every 7.5 m of lateral travel
Projecting 1 m above the edge, every 15 m of lateral travel
Projecting 1.5 m above the edge, at each end only
source: Cl. 5.4 i): ladder projecting minimum 1 m above the edge; ladders every 7.5 m (25 ft) of lateral travel, secured top and bottom.

q: For an excavation up to 1.2 m deep, what is the minimum distance excavated material (spoil) must be placed from the edge?
source: Cl. 5.4 l): excavated material shall be placed not less than 1 m from the edge for depth up to 1.2 m, increased in proportion to depth.

q: Heavy equipment, materials and excavating machinery must be kept at least how far from the excavation area?
source: Cl. 5.4 n): heavy equipment, material or excavating machinery shall be kept clear from the excavation area by at least 3 m.

q: Which barricading arrangement around an open trench meets KOC.SA.026?
options: Barrier tape tied between steel rebars
Hard fixed barriers with reflective warning signs
Rope strung between rebars at each corner
Spoil heaped along the edge as a bund
source: Cl. 4.3 / 5.4 k): hard fixed barriers with reflective warning notices, signs and flashing lights; tapes and rebars shall not be used as barriers.

q: An excavation in Type B soil will exceed 1 m in depth. Which shoring arrangement meets KOC.SA.026?
options: No shoring if the sides are sloped at 30°
Sheeting 450 mm above ground; boards ≤ 750 mm apart
Polling boards 2 m apart; braces 2 m apart
No shoring if the trench is under 2 m deep
source: Cl. 5.6.1.2 a): Type B over 1 m — shoring required; sheeting at least 450 mm above ground; polling boards ≤ 750 mm apart; horizontal braces ≤ 1 m apart.

q: In addition to the Excavation Notification, which work permit is required for excavation using a mechanical excavator?
source: Cl. 5.3 e) / 5.6.2: a Hot Work Permit is required for excavation involving a mechanical excavator; a Cold Work Permit for manual excavation.

q: In addition to the Excavation Notification, which permit is required for MANUAL excavation with hand tools?
source: Cl. 4.1 / 5.3 e): Cold Work Permit for manual excavation; Hot Work Permit for mechanical excavation.

q: Which clearance must be obtained before any excavation work in a KOC area?
options: Fire Team training certificate for crew
Municipality building permit for the site
source: Cl. 5.4 a): no excavation work in KOC area shall be undertaken without ensuring EOD clearance for that location.

q: Why must a shovel with a metal handle NOT be used for manual excavation?
options: It rusts quickly in damp soil
Electrocution if a live cable is struck
It damages the soil layers below
It is heavier to lift all day long
source: Cl. 5.4 w): shovel with metal handle shall not be used for manual excavation to prevent the risk of electrocution.

q: In Type A (cohesive) soil, up to what depth is shoring usually NOT required?
source: Cl. 5.6.1.1 a): for Type A soil, shoring is not usually required provided the depth does not exceed 1 m.

q: In Type A soil where space permits, to what angle may the sides be sloped to excavate deeper without shoring?
source: Cl. 5.6.1.1 b): if surface area permits, greater depth can be made by sloping the side down to an angle of 45°.

q: What support is required for excavation in Type C soil, such as sand or soil with water seeping?
options: No support if under 2 m deep
source: Cl. 5.6.1.3: in Type C or poor soil, close sheeting or a continued series of polling boards shall be used.

q: Under KOC.SA.026, a trench is a narrow excavation whose bottom width is NOT greater than:
source: Cl. 2.0: the width of a trench (measured at the bottom) is not greater than 15 ft (4.6 m).

q: Why must equipment with internal combustion engines NOT be kept inside an excavation?
options: It raises the noise above 85 dB
It blocks the ladder access route
It may sink into the soft soil
Exhaust gases such as CO build up
source: Cl. 5.4 t): such equipment shall not be kept inside the excavation to prevent accumulation of CO and CO2.

q: In what layer thickness should excavations be backfilled and rammed?
source: Cl. 5.6.5: excavations shall be backfilled in 150 mm layers and solidly rammed and tamped.

q: Contaminated soil is found in a spoil heap. How may it be used?
options: Used for the top 150 mm layer only
Mixed 50/50 with clean soil for backfill
Not used; disposed of per KOC.EV.008
Used if covered with plastic sheeting
source: Cl. 5.6.5: no contaminated soil shall be used for backfilling; it shall be disposed of per KOC.EV.008.

q: May a mechanical excavator dig while workers are inside the trench?
options: Yes, if a banksman is present
Yes, if they stay 2 m from the bucket
No, never while personnel are inside
Yes, for the final 0.5 m only
source: Cl. 5.6.2 e): mechanical excavation shall not be carried out while personnel are inside the trench / excavation.

q: Excavation work may affect the bund wall of a crude oil storage tank. Who must additionally endorse the Excavation Notification?
source: Cl. 4.7 / 5.3 d): for bund wall cutting or excavation affecting the bunded area, the Excavation Notification shall be endorsed by the Fire Team.

q: What must be done with the bucket of a loader or backhoe when it is not in operation?
options: Rest it on the spoil heap edge
source: Cl. 5.6.2 g): the bucket must always be lowered to the ground if the loader or backhoe is not in operation.

q: How does KOC.SA.027 define 'High Voltage'?
options: A system voltage of 1000 V and above
A system voltage of 3300 V and above
source: Cl. 2.0: High Voltage – a system voltage of 3300 volts and above; Low Voltage – not exceeding 440 volts.

q: Portable tools and extension cords above 50 V to ground that are frequently plugged and unplugged must be protected by an RCD with a maximum trip setting of:
source: Cl. 5.1: such equipment must be protected by permanent or portable RCDs with a 30 mA maximum current setting.

q: A crane must pass under an existing 132 kV overhead power line. What is the minimum vertical clearance required between the lowest conductor and the top of the equipment?
source: Cl. 5.1 table: for 33 kV & 132 kV lines, minimum vertical safety clearance from lowest conductor to top of equipment is 5 m (10 m from ground).

q: A portable hand lamp on a trailing lead is needed inside a confined space. What does KOC.SA.027 require?
options: Supply not exceeding 24 V and explosion-proof type
Supply not exceeding 110 V with an RCD
Supply not exceeding 240 V with double insulation
Any lamp, if the space is gas free
source: Cl. 5.2: for a portable hand lamp on a trailing lead inside a confined space, supply voltage shall not exceed 24 V and only explosion-proof type shall be used.

q: When an isolated LV/HV conductor is earthed by installing a copper earthing conductor, what is its minimum cross-section?
source: Cl. 5.3 C: each conductor shall be earthed by fixed earthing switch, CB, or a copper conductor of minimum cross section 25 sq. mm.

q: Before starting work inside a substation protected by a CO2 or clean-agent suppression system, what must the authorized electrical person do?
options: Disable the fire alarm panel for the whole shift
Switch the system to Manual/Maintenance mode
Open all doors so any released gas can escape
Keep the system on Auto and wear an SCBA set
source: Cl. 4.4 / 5.3 A: turn the system to Manual/Maintenance mode on entry and return it to Normal (Auto) mode after the job and evacuation; record in the logbook.

q: A worker is unconscious and still in contact with an electrical source. What does KOC.SA.027 say should be done first?
options: Pull the victim away by the clothing
Free the victim using a Rescue Stick
Pour water on the equipment to trip it
source: Cl. 5.2: the victim should be removed safely from the electrical source by means of a Rescue Stick and artificial respiration given by trained personnel.

q: Under the 'Test Before Touch' requirement of KOC.SA.027, how must the voltage tester itself be checked?
options: Only once a year when it is calibrated
On a known live source before and after use
Only before use, with its self-test button
Not needed when the tester is brand new
source: Cl. 5.1: Test Before Touch includes verifying test instruments on a known energized source before and after the test for absence of voltage.

q: Before cutting an isolated high voltage cable, what must be done at the point of cut?
options: Wrap the cable with insulating tape
Spike it with a spiking gun or earthed spike
Test insulation resistance at 5 kV first
Hang a caution notice at the cut point
source: Cl. 5.3 D: HV cables shall be spiked at the point where they are to be cut by a spiking gun or a wooden-shafted, earthed steel-shod spike.

q: How does KOC.SA.027 define 'Low Voltage'?
source: Cl. 2.0: Low Voltage — a system voltage not exceeding 440 volts.

q: Until proven otherwise with a meter or tester, electrical equipment must be considered:
source: Cl. 2.0: all electrical equipment are considered to be energized until proven otherwise (using a meter / tester).

q: Under KOC.SA.027, work on electrical circuitry must NOT be carried out by:
source: Cl. 5.2: any works on electrical circuitry should not be conducted by a single or lone person.

q: Which plugs and sockets must be used at KOC locations other than offices and houses?
source: Cl. 4.3 / 5.2: only industrial type plugs and sockets shall be used on all locations other than offices and houses.

q: What minimum vertical clearance is required between a 400 kV overhead line and the top of passing equipment?
source: Cl. 5.1 table: 400 kV — 7 m minimum vertical clearance from lowest conductor to top of equipment (12 m from ground).

q: What minimum vertical clearance is required between a 3.3 kV overhead line and the top of passing equipment?
source: Cl. 5.1 table: 3.3 kV — 2 m clearance to top of equipment; 5 m clearance from ground.

q: When a new asphalt road is built under an existing overhead line, what height barriers does KOC.SA.027 (MEW requirement) specify?
options: 7 m high, in each direction of traffic
5 m high, in each direction of traffic
source: Cl. 5.1: height barriers of 5 m height shall be installed in each direction of traffic.

q: A small fire starts on an electrical panel. What is the correct first action?
options: Isolate the supply, then use an extinguisher
Wait for the Fire Team without acting
Open the panel door to inspect the fire
Spray water on the panel straight away
source: Cl. 5.2: in the event of fire on electrical panel, the power supply must be isolated and a suitable extinguisher used.

q: During work inside a substation, where must the authorized electrical person be?
options: In the substation for the whole job
In the control room, on the radio
At site only at start and finish
source: Cl. 5.3 A: the authorized electrical person shall remain present in the substation during the entire work period.

q: Where work on a live LV cable is unavoidable, how many conductors may be bared at a time?
options: All, if insulated gloves are worn
source: Cl. 5.3 F: only one conductor should be bared at a time, with rubber boots, mats or gloves.

q: Which type of ladder must NOT be used for electrical work or in substations?
source: Cl. 5.2: portable metal ladders / stepladders should not be used for electrical work or in substations.

q: In an emergency, who may isolate a low or high voltage switch?
source: Cl. 5.3 B: in an emergency, anyone may isolate a LV / HV switch; such action must be immediately reported to the respective authority.

q: After work on isolated HV apparatus is complete and earths are removed, what test should be carried out before re-energizing?
source: Cl. 5.3 C: remove earth connections and perform an Insulation Resistance test before voltage test or re-energizing; discharge equipment after the test.

q: A single crane will lift a load equal to 80% of its rated capacity at the planned radius. Under KOC.SA.029, this lift is:
options: A standard lift, since it is below 100% of capacity
A critical lift, because it exceeds 75% of rated capacity
A critical lift only if it also exceeds 50 tonnes
A standard lift if it is done in daylight
source: Cl. 2.0 Critical lift: loads exceeding 75% of the rated capacity of any one crane.

q: Which of the following lifts is classified as a critical lift by height under KOC.SA.029?
options: A lift exceeding 10 m in height
A lift exceeding 20 m in height
A lift exceeding 30 m in height
A lift exceeding 50 m in height
source: Cl. 2.0 Critical lift: lifts which exceed 30 m in height (also > 50 tonnes, > 75% capacity, multiple cranes, man-lifting, etc.).

q: What is the minimum age for an operator of load handling equipment under KOC.SA.029?
source: Cl. 2.0 Operator: should be minimum 21 years of age, with 3rd party training certificates for the equipment.

q: A lifting sling is inspected in November. According to the KOC.SA.029 quarterly colour code, which colour should it carry?
source: Cl. 5.2: Q1 Apr–Jun Green; Q2 Jul–Sep Yellow; Q3 Oct–Dec Blue; Q4 Jan–Mar White.

q: Above what wind speed at the personnel platform must a man-lifting operation not begin, or be terminated if in progress?
source: Cl. 5.6.5: when wind speed exceeds 15 mph (24 km/h) at the personnel platform, man-lifting must not begin or must be terminated.

q: What minimum size of outrigger pad does KOC.SA.029 recommend under each crane outrigger float?
options: Same size as the outrigger foot
At least twice the size of the outrigger foot
At least three times the size of the outrigger foot
At least five times the size of the outrigger foot
source: Cl. 5.6.3: outrigger pad size should be at least three times the size of the outrigger foot.

q: When must a wire rope be removed from service due to broken wires under KOC.SA.029?
options: When any single broken wire is found
When broken wires exceed 10% in 8 diameters
When broken wires exceed 25% in one lay
Only when a full strand is broken
source: Cl. 5.8.3: wire rope shall not be used if, in any length of eight diameters, total visible broken wires exceed 10% of total wires.

q: What is the maximum speed at which material handling equipment (e.g. a forklift) may be driven while operating inside a company facility?
source: Cl. 5.8.4: the equipment shall not be driven at a speed exceeding 8 km per hour while operating in a company facility.

q: A contractor installs a fixed tower crane at a KOC site. What is the maximum validity of the Controlling Team's approval before the approval process must be repeated?
source: Cl. 5.3: approval for contractor fixed / permanently installed load handling equipment shall not exceed 12 months.

q: A planned lift weighs 60 tonnes using one crane well within its capacity. How is it classified?
options: Standard lift, as it is within capacity
Critical lift, because it exceeds 50 tonnes
Standard lift if done in daylight
source: Cl. 2.0 Critical lift: lifts that exceed 50 tonnes in weight.

q: How many banksmen should the crane operator take signals from at any time?
options: Whoever is closest to the cab
source: Cl. 5.6.3: the operator shall respond only to signals from one banksman who shall be clearly identified.

q: How should a suspended load be controlled to prevent swinging?
options: By a worker holding the load by hand
source: Cl. 5.6.3: the load should be controlled using two guide ropes (tag lines) of adequate strength.

q: What is the typical maximum in-service wind speed for mobile cranes given in KOC.SA.029?
source: Cl. 5.6.5: typical maximum in-service wind speed is 35 km/h for mobile cranes and 72 km/h for tower cranes.

q: What minimum passageway must be kept between the slewing parts of a crane and nearby guardrails or fixtures?
source: Cl. 5.6.3: a passageway of minimum 610 mm shall be maintained between slewing / moving parts and guardrails / fixtures.

q: Is anyone allowed to ride on a load or hook suspended from a crane?
options: Yes, for short lifts under 2 m
source: Cl. 5.6.3: it is strictly prohibited for anybody to ride on loads, buckets or hooks suspended from a crane.

q: Who carries out the daily inspection of a crane at the start of each shift?
source: Cl. 4.6 / 5.9.1: daily and weekly inspection shall be carried out by the load handling equipment operator.

q: For how long must records of daily crane inspections be kept?
source: Cl. 5.9.2: daily inspection records maintained for 15 days (weekly inspection records for 30 days).

q: What is the minimum number of full tucks in an eye splice made in a wire rope?
source: Cl. 5.8.3: an eye splice made in any wire rope shall have not less than three full tucks.

q: A sling is slightly too long. How may it be shortened?
options: Tie a single knot in one leg
Clamp the extra length with a bolt
Do not shorten it with knots or loops
Wrap it twice around the hook
source: Cl. 5.8.2: sling shall not be shortened with knots, bolts or other makeshift devices or by looping around a crane hook.

q: Why does KOC.SA.029 say wet webbing slings should not be used?
options: They become too heavy to handle
They cannot then be colour coded
source: Cl. 5.8.2: do not use wet webbing slings since it will reduce the sling rated capacity.

q: What should be done when a load is first lifted?
options: Lift just clear, stop and check
Lift with people steadying it below
Swing it straight to the landing
source: Cl. 5.6.3: the load shall initially be lifted just clear of the supporting surface and brought to rest while slings and balance are checked.

q: May lifting equipment be used to drag a load along the ground?
options: Yes, with a tag line attached
Yes, if the hoist rope stays vertical
source: Cl. 5.6.3: lifting equipment shall not be used for dragging load.

q: Unless conditions warrant greater clearance, painting should not be carried out within what distance of potential ignition sources such as welding or flame cutting?
source: Cl. 5.10: no painting should be carried out within 75 feet of potential ignition sources.

q: Which surface preparation method is prohibited under KOC.SA.030?
source: Cl. 5.4: sand blasting is prohibited.

q: Which of the following must NOT be used for solvent cleaning of surfaces before painting?
options: Alkali cleaners from an approved supplier
source: Cl. 5.4: benzene, gasoline, carbon tetrachloride and chlorinated hydrocarbons with low TLVs (< 20 ppm) shall not be used for solvent cleaning.

q: If practical alternatives exist, solvents and paints shall not be applied to surfaces warmer than:
source: Cl. 5.10: solvents and paints shall not be applied to surfaces warmer than 80°C if practical alternatives exist (and not flushed into containers hotter than 50°C).

q: A painter suffers a small skin puncture from high-pressure fluid from an airless spray gun. What does KOC.SA.030 require?
options: Clean with solvent and apply a plaster
Continue work and report at the end of shift
Wash with soap and monitor for 24 hours
source: Cl. 5.5: emergency medical care shall be obtained immediately if any high pressure fluid penetrates the skin; injection injuries can be extremely serious.

q: Inside a confined space, during which activities must all personnel wear respirable air-fed hoods under KOC.SA.030?
options: Only during abrasive blasting of surfaces
Only during airless spray painting work
During blasting, spraying, solvent or brush work
Only when the LEL reading exceeds 10%
source: Cl. 5.8: air-fed hoods shall be worn inside confined spaces whenever blasting or spray painting, solvent cleaning or brush painting is in progress.

q: Where should paint or thinner be decanted from one container to another?
options: Inside the store, near the shelves
In the open air, away from hazardous operations
Inside the spray booth, exhaust running
At the work face, beside the item painted
source: Cl. 5.11: dispensing or decanting shall not take place within the store but in the open air away from areas of hazardous operations.

q: What must be done whenever an airless spray gun is left unattended?
options: Point the gun into the paint bucket
source: Cl. 5.5: the trigger safety catch shall be engaged whenever the airless gun is left unattended; tip guard always in place while spraying.

q: Where practicable, from which side of the object should spray painting be done?
source: Cl. 5.5: spray painting should be conducted from the upwind side of the object being coated, wherever practicable.

q: Where may food be eaten under KOC.SA.030?
options: Not where paint is stored, handled or used
At the work face during breaks
In the paint store if the lids are closed
In the spray booth after spraying
source: Cl. 5.7: food shall not be brought into or consumed on premises where paint is stored, handled or used.

q: A painter has paint on his hands. How should he clean his skin?
options: With the cleaning solvent used for spray guns
With thinner from the paint store
With special skin cleansers, not solvents
source: Cl. 5.7: solvents shall not be used for cleansing the skin; special skin cleansers shall be provided.

q: Solvents shall not be flushed into containers hotter than:
source: Cl. 5.10: solvents shall not be flushed into containers that are hotter than 50°C.

q: What must be done with switches, panel boards and motors in the area before spray painting?
source: Cl. 5.10: all electrical equipment such as switches, panel boards and motors must be de-energized before spray painting.

q: While painting is in progress inside a confined space, hot work inside the same space is:
source: Cl. 5.9: hot work shall not be permitted inside the confined space during painting works.

q: What is the minimum number of persons that should work together when painting inside a confined space?
source: Cl. 5.9: there should be minimum two persons to work in confined spaces.

q: When should gas testing be carried out for painting work under KOC.SA.030?
options: Only if a smell is noticed
Only at the end of the shift
source: Cl. 5.1: gas test should be carried out per KOC.HE.003 before and after painting works.

q: What safety device must be provided at the nozzle end of an abrasive blasting hose?
options: Flashback arrestor at the blast pot
Spark guard fitted on the nozzle tip
Pressure gauge fitted at the nozzle
source: Cl. 5.6: a dead man control device shall be provided at the nozzle end of the blasting hose.

q: May extension cords or plug-in cords be used inside a spray paint booth?
options: Yes, if taped at the joints
No, they should not be used
source: Cl. 5.10: extension cords or other electrical plug-in cords should not be used in a spray paint booth.

q: How often must the fit test of a painter's respirator be repeated?
source: Cl. 5.8 a): ensure the respirator is fit tested first and thereafter repeated at least annually.

q: What must be marked on containers of lead-based paint?
options: The painter's name and KOC ID
source: Cl. 5.11: receptacles containing lead based paint must be legibly marked to alert about lead hazard.

q: Under KOC.SA.031, an activity is defined as 'work at height' when it is carried out at an elevated location higher than:
source: Cl. 2.0: work at height is an activity at an elevated location of more than 1.8 m (6 ft) from the working ground level.

q: What minimum load must a fixed anchor point be capable of supporting for each person attached to it?
source: Cl. 2.0 / 5.2.3.3: an anchorage must be capable of supporting at least 5,000 lb (22.2 kN) for each person attached.

q: Which lanyard specification complies with KOC.SA.031 for use with a full body harness?
options: Max 1.8 m, shock absorber, self-locking hooks
Max 3 m, made of polypropylene rope
Any length, shortened by tying knots
source: Cl. 5.2.3.2: maximum lanyard length 1.8 m (6 ft), self-locking hooks each end, shock absorber; never shortened with knots; no polypropylene.

q: As a general guideline, at what length of climb on a fixed ladder must appropriate fall protection be provided?
source: Cl. 5.2.2: appropriate fall protection must be provided whenever the length of climb on a fixed ladder equals or exceeds 24 ft (7.3 m).

q: Which guardrail arrangement meets the KOC.SA.031 edge protection requirements?
options: Top rail 750 mm high; no mid rail needed
Top rail ≥ 950 mm; no gap over 470 mm
Top rail 1,200 mm; gaps up to 600 mm
Steel banding as top rail at 1,000 mm
source: Cl. 5.2.1 / 5.2.3.8: main guard rail at least 950 mm (normally 1,000 mm); no gap more than 470 mm; steel/plastic banding not permitted as rails.

q: Which statement about personal fall arrest equipment is correct under KOC.SA.031?
options: A body belt may be used if it has a shock absorber
Body belts are prohibited; harness with 100% tie-off
100% tie-off is needed only above 6 m in height
One lanyard is enough when moving between anchors
source: Cl. 5.2.3.1: full body harness with two shock-absorbing lanyards; use of a body belt for fall arrest is prohibited; ensure 100% tie-off.

q: In addition to the user's visual pre-use check, how often must the Controlling Team ensure harnesses, lanyards and lifelines are formally inspected and tagged?
source: Cl. 5.3: all fall-arresting equipment shall be subjected to a monthly inspection program and tagged if fit for use.

q: A worker's lanyard arrested a short fall, and the shock absorber appears undamaged. What does KOC.SA.031 require?
options: Re-use it after a careful visual check
Re-use it after re-packing the absorber
Use it for work restraint only
source: Cl. 5.2.3.2 / 5.3: components subjected to impact loading shall be removed from service; equipment involved in a fall must not be used again.

q: Use of a crane-suspended man basket to lift workers is permitted only in exceptional cases. How must the lift be classified and planned?
options: As a standard lift with a JSA only
As a critical lift with a Critical Lift Plan
As routine work not requiring a permit
As a standard lift if fitted with guardrails
source: Cl. 5.2.2: use of a man basket shall be considered a critical lift; a Critical Lift Plan shall be prepared per KOC.SA.029.

q: According to the work-at-height hierarchy of controls, what is the FIRST approach?
source: Cl. 5.1: fall elimination first, then fall prevention, then fall arresting as the last line of defence.

q: What must a worker do with his safety helmet while climbing a ladder or working at height?
source: Cl. 5.2.2: the worker must wear the chin strap of the safety helmet to prevent its fall from the head.

q: At what interval of vertical climb must an appropriate landing place be provided?
source: Cl. 5.2.2: a landing place of adequate size and strength shall be provided at every 30 ft (9 m) of vertical climb.

q: How many persons may use a single vertical lifeline at the same time?
source: Cl. 5.2.3.4: a vertical lifeline shall be used by only one person at a time.

q: What minimum breaking strength must a vertical lifeline (drop line) have?
source: Cl. 2.0: drop line must have a minimum breaking strength of 5,400 lb or 2,450 kg (OSHA 1926.104).

q: Where should an anchor point for a lanyard be positioned?
source: Cl. 5.2.3.3: anchoring point always shall be above shoulder level.

q: How often must safety nets be inspected for wear, damage and deterioration?
source: Cl. 5.2.3.7: safety nets shall be inspected at least once a week.

q: How often must a standalone guardrail (not part of a scaffold) be inspected and tagged?
options: Before first use, then every 7 days
Every 3 months, by a third party
source: Cl. 5.2.3.8: standalone guardrails inspected before first use and every seven (7) days; a tag affixed.

q: A guardrail top rail must withstand a force applied outward or downward of at least:
source: Cl. 5.2.3.8: guardrail system must withstand at least 200 lb (about 890 N) applied within 2 inches of the top edge.

q: Two crews plan to work at height at different levels directly above one another. Under KOC.SA.031 this is:
options: Not allowed, due to falling objects
Allowed if both crews wear helmets
Allowed if upper crew uses tool lanyards
source: Cl. 5.2.1: simultaneous work at height shall not be allowed at multiple levels to avoid 'struck by falling object'.

q: What is the minimum age for a person working on a suspended working platform (gondola)?
source: Cl. 5.2.2 b): every person on the working platform should be at least 18 years old, fit, agile and not suffer from acrophobia.

q: Which material must NOT be used for lanyards and lifelines?
source: Cl. 5.2.3.2: manila, other natural fibres and polypropylene must not be used; nylon, Dacron, webbing or aircraft cable may be used.

q: What is the minimum rope diameter for use with a rope grab under KOC.SA.031?
source: Cl. 5.2.3.5: the minimum diameter for rope grab shall be 1.59 cm (5/8 inch rope).

q: In a cylinder store, oxygen cylinders must be separated from fuel-gas cylinders by a minimum of:
options: 3 m, or a 1 m high barrier
6.1 m, or a 1.5 m high fire-rated barrier
10 m, with no barrier option allowed
15 m, or any solid wall of any height
source: Cl. 5.4: oxygen separated from fuel-gas cylinders by at least 20 ft (6.1 m) or a non-combustible barrier at least 5 ft (1.5 m) high, ½-hour fire resistance.

q: According to the hose colour coding in KOC.SA.035 (BS EN ISO 3821), which colour hose is used for acetylene?
source: Cl. 5.7: Blue – Oxygen; Red – Acetylene; Orange – Propane, LPG, Natural Gas or Fuel Gas.

q: Compressed gas cylinders must not be exposed to temperatures (including direct sunlight) exceeding:
source: Cl. 5.4: any cylinder containing compressed gas shall not be subjected to a temperature exceeding 54.5°C (130°F).

q: Why must acetylene cylinders be stored, handled and used in the vertical position?
options: To let the porous mass settle evenly
To stop liquid acetone escaping to the valve
To keep the cylinder cooler in sunlight
To make the colour code easier to read
source: Cl. 5.1: acetylene is dissolved in acetone; cylinders must be kept vertical to prevent liquid acetone escaping and damaging valves and equipment.

q: As a means of distinguishing gases, which valve outlet thread is used on acetylene, hydrogen and other flammable gas cylinders?
source: Cl. 5.2: right-hand thread for oxygen and non-flammable gases; left-hand thread for acetylene, hydrogen and flammable gases.

q: A flashback occurs during oxy-acetylene cutting, but the hose looks intact from outside. What must be done with the hose?
options: Purge it with oxygen and continue the job
Leak test with soapy water and re-use if OK
Discard it immediately; the inner wall is damaged
Cut off the last metre and re-use the rest
source: Cl. 5.7: any hose in which a flashback has occurred will have its inner wall damaged and must be discarded immediately.

q: After opening a gas cylinder valve fully for use, how should it be left?
options: Fully open against the back stop
A half turn back from full open
Fully open and taped in position
source: Cl. 5.5: an open valve shall be left a half turn back from full open so that movement to the back stop indicates the valve is open.

q: 'Snifting' (briefly opening a cylinder valve to clear dirt before fitting a regulator) is permitted for most gases. For which gas is it NEVER allowed?
source: Cl. 5.5: hydrogen shall never be snifted as it may ignite spontaneously.

q: What colour hose is used for oxygen under KOC.SA.035?
source: Cl. 5.7: Blue – Oxygen; Red – Acetylene; Orange – Propane / LPG / fuel gas.

q: How must gas cylinder connections be checked for leaks?
options: A lighted match held near the joint
An oily cloth wiped over the joint
Soapy water or approved leak spray
source: Cl. 5.5: leak tests with mild soapy water or approved leak detection spray and NEVER by a naked flame.

q: May a 12 kg domestic LPG cooking cylinder be used for pre-heating a pipeline?
options: Yes, with a fire extinguisher nearby
Yes, if a regulator is fitted
No, domestic cylinders are not allowed
source: Cl. 5.5: LPG cylinders intended for domestic purposes such as cooking shall not be used for welding, pre-heating or heating.

q: Flammable substances shall not be stored within what distance of a gas cylinder storage area?
source: Cl. 5.4: flammable substances shall not be stored within 50 ft (15.25 m) of cylinder storage areas.

q: If oxygen cylinders are stacked horizontally, what is the maximum number per tier?
source: Cl. 5.4: horizontal stacking in pyramid shape with not more than 15 numbers to a single tier; largest at the bottom.

q: When cylinders are placed directly on forklift forks, how much of the fork length may they occupy?
source: Cl. 5.3: cylinders may be placed directly on the forks provided no more than 80% of the fork length is occupied.

q: How should a gas cylinder be lifted by crane?
options: Slung with a chain round the body
Hooked by its valve or nozzle
source: Cl. 5.3: never lifted by valves, magnets or chains; strapped securely in a cradle.

q: How should an oxy-acetylene torch be lit?
options: Acetylene first, with a friction lighter
Both gases together, with a cigarette lighter
source: Cl. 5.5 / 5.7: safe ignition with a friction lighter; torches are lit on acetylene first and oxygen used to adjust the flame.

q: How far must an oxyacetylene blowpipe or other ignition source be kept from the oxygen and acetylene cylinders?
source: Cl. 5.5: blowpipe or approved ignition source kept at a distance of more than 5 m (16 ft) from acetylene and oxygen cylinders.

q: What minimum maximum-dial reading must a contents gauge for an oxygen cylinder have?
source: Cl. 5.6: gauges for oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen cylinders: max dial reading not less than 225 bar (acetylene: 40 bar).

q: May full or empty oxygen and acetylene cylinders be transported alongside each other?
options: Yes, if valve caps are fitted
source: Cl. 5.3: oxygen and acetylene cylinders shall not be transported or stored alongside one another whether empty or full.

q: How long must inspection records for cylinders, regulators, hoses and torches be retained?
source: Cl. 8.0: inspection records — six (6) months; test certificates — five years.

q: According to KOC.HE.003, what is the permissible flammable gas limit for authorized cold work?
source: Cl. 5.6.1: the permissible limit for authorized cold work is below 10% of the LEL (hot work: 0% LEL).

q: Where periodic gas testing is used during hot or cold work, the test interval must not exceed:
source: Cl. 5.6.1 / 5.6.3: testing continuously or periodically with the test interval not exceeding two hours.

q: When gas testing for hot work, the gas test area shall include everywhere within what distance of the hot work location?
source: Cl. 5.7: the gas test area shall include everywhere within 50 ft (15 m) of the hot work location.

q: A confined space is being mechanically ventilated by an exhaust fan. When should the gas test be carried out?
options: While the fan is running at full speed
Immediately after switching the fan off
About 10 minutes after stopping the exhaust fan
Only after the fan has been removed from the manway
source: Cl. 5.7: for a mechanically ventilated confined space, test only after 10 minutes of stopping the exhaust fan to avoid the effect of air draft.

q: Which acceptable exposure levels (TLV-TWA) does KOC.HE.003 state for carbon monoxide and sulphur dioxide?
source: Cl. 5.3: acceptable levels — carbon monoxide 25 ppm (TLV-TWA, ACGIH) and sulphur dioxide 5 ppm (TLV-TWA, KEPA).

q: Under the TLV-STEL definition in KOC.HE.003, exposures above the TLV-TWA up to the STEL should be:
options: Less than 15 minutes each, no more than 4 times a day, at least 60 minutes apart
Less than 30 minutes each, no more than 2 times a day, at least 30 minutes apart
Less than 15 minutes each, unlimited times a day
Less than 60 minutes each, once a day
source: Cl. 2.0: exposures above TWA up to STEL should be < 15 minutes, no more than four times per day, with at least 60 minutes between them.

q: Which type of portable gas detector must be used for all INITIAL gas tests under KOC.HE.003?
options: Aspirated monitor with built-in sampling pump
Single-gas H2S badge clipped on the collar
Fixed area gas detector at the facility
source: Cl. 5.4.1: aspirated gas monitors (built-in pump) — all initial gas tests shall be done with this type of detector.

q: When testing a vessel where H2S could be present, where is it essential to sample?
options: As close to the top of the vessel as possible
Only at the manway opening of the vessel
As close to the bottom of the vessel as possible
Only through the vessel's vent line
source: Cl. 5.5 / 5.7: H2S is heavier than air (1.19); sample as close to the bottom as possible.

q: A gas detector is taken from an air-conditioned office to a hot outdoor worksite. What does KOC.HE.003 advise before using it?
options: Use it immediately, as sensors are temperature compensated
Allow 5–30 minutes for the instrument to stabilize to the temperature
Re-calibrate it in the field with test gas every time
Keep it in a plastic bag to avoid condensation during the test
source: Cl. 5.1: allow sufficient time for the equipment to temperature stabilize prior to use, which may vary between 5–30 minutes.

q: What oxygen range does KOC.HE.003 state is required in the atmosphere tested?
source: Cl. 5.3: oxygen is normally 21%; required O2 is between 19.5% and 23.5%.

q: Who carries out gas tests for work permits under KOC.HE.003?
source: Cl. 4.2 / 5.1: gas testing is carried out by Authorized Gas Testers, with results recorded on the permit.

q: What is a 'bump test' of a gas detector?
options: A drop test to check the casing
A quick pre-use check with test gas
A check of battery charge level
source: Cl. 2.0: bump test — a quick functional test with a standard sample carried out prior to use (see KOC.GE.036).

q: The calibration gas cylinder is past its expiry date. What does KOC.HE.003 say?
options: Never use test gas after its expiry
Use it while the cylinder is full
Use it if the readings look normal
Use it for bump tests only
source: Cl. 5.4.2: only use certified traceable test gas before its expiration date; never use a test gas after expiry.

q: Who shall perform the calibration and certification of portable gas detectors (PGDs)?
options: Any trained operator on the site
The Permit Applicant for the job
source: Cl. 5.4.2: manufacturer or an accredited third party shall perform the calibration and certification of PGDs.

q: Before using a portable gas detector, what must the user confirm on its calibration label?
options: Calibration expiry is after the issue date
The detector has been used at least once
Label colour matches the work area zone
The battery brand is on the approved list
source: Cl. 4.2 / 5.4: each PGD has a legible calibration label and the calibration expiry date is later than the issue date.

q: When testing a confined space for a gas that is LIGHTER than air, such as acetylene, where should you test?
source: Cl. 5.7: test as low as possible for heavier gases and as high as possible for gases lighter than air (e.g. CO 0.97, acetylene 0.91).

q: Where should the contents of a pipe be gas tested before it is broken into?
options: At the nearest storage tank vent outlet
Anywhere at all along the same line
As near the break-in point as possible
At the control room's fixed gas analyser
source: Cl. 5.5: test from a sampling point as near to the break-in point as possible, or on either side of it.

q: A multi-gas detector is shared among several users. What should be done before each use?
options: Clean or disinfect it per the maker
Nothing, if the battery is charged
source: Cl. 5.1: a portable multi gas detector shared among multiple users should be disinfected / cleaned before use per manufacturer's recommendation.

q: Who is the custodian of portable gas detectors, responsible for issuing them and ensuring timely maintenance and calibration?
source: Cl. 4.3: the Authorized Gas Tester is the custodian of all portable gas detectors, their issuance and timely maintenance and calibration.

q: A tank atmosphere is above the Upper Explosive Limit (UEL). Why is this NOT a safe condition?
options: It is too lean to burn
Air ingress can make it flammable
It only affects toxic gas readings
It cannot be measured at all
source: Cl. 2.0: above UEL is 'too rich' to burn, but not a good basis for safety as added oxygen brings it into the flammable region.

q: Who states on the Work Permit how long a gas test remains valid before a new test is required?
source: Cl. 4.3: the authorized gas tester states on the Work Permit how long the test is valid before a new gas test is required.

q: Why should only manufacturer-approved sampling lines be used with a gas detector?
options: They may contain silicone that poisons sensors
Non-approved lines are too heavy to carry
Approved lines remove the need to calibrate
Approved lines are always much shorter
source: Cl. 5.1: a non-approved sampling line may contain silicone compounds which may poison the sensors.

q: A contractor has 120 workers at a site. Under KOC.HE.004, what is the minimum number of first aiders required?
source: Cl. 5.4.1 c): one first aider per every 50 employees / contract workers (minimum one). 120 workers → 3 first aiders.

q: What is the required provision of first aid kits under KOC.HE.004?
options: One kit per facility, regardless of numbers
source: Cl. 5.5 / 5.8: one first aid kit shall be made available for every 50 workers.

q: To remain appropriately qualified, how often must a KOC first aider attend a first aid refresher course?
source: Cl. 5.5 B: first aiders attend refresher training courses every three (3) years.

q: How often must designated first aiders attend a CPR and AED training session?
source: Cl. 5.5 B / 5.6.1: attend CPR & AED training session once every year.

q: Under KOC.HE.004 and Kuwait labour requirements, a contractor must establish a First Aid Room wherever how many workers are engaged?
source: Cl. 5.4.1 a) / 5.5 II A: a First Aid Room shall be established wherever fifty (50) or more workers are engaged.

q: Which statement about first aid kit containers is correct under KOC.HE.004?
options: Locked, to prevent theft of contents
Clearly labelled, visible and not locked
Opened only by the site medic
source: Cl. 5.8.1: the first aid container should be prominently displayed, labelled 'First Aid Box', accessible, and should not be locked.

q: Within what time must a first aid case be reported in MyHSSE under KOC.HE.004 (with KOC.GE.007)?
source: Cl. 4: report in MyHSSE within 24 hours of incident occurrence (as per KOC.GE.007 & KOC.HE.020).

q: Which statement best describes the role of a first aider under KOC.HE.004?
options: Give initial care within training; refer to medical advice
Provide ongoing treatment until full recovery
Prescribe medicines from the first aid kit stock
Decide whether the injury needs to be reported
source: Cl. 5.6: first aiders undertake initial treatment consistent with training; when in doubt recommend medical advice; not responsible for ongoing care.

q: What minimum first aid cover must Team Leaders ensure in each work area or operating facility?
options: One first aider per facility for all shifts
One first aider per day shift only
At least one first aider per shift
A first aider only when 50 workers are present
source: Cl. 4.6: ensure at least one first aider per shift in each work area / operation facility.

q: How often must a First Aid Needs Assessment be reviewed, unless changes occur earlier?
source: Cl. 5.3: assessments made initially and reviewed once in three years, or earlier if layout, staff numbers or hazards change.

q: What does an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) do?
source: Cl. 2.2: AED analyzes the heartbeat, advises action and delivers a calibrated electric shock.

q: Which qualification meets KOC.HE.004 requirements for a Contractor Medic?
options: Driving licence and a basic first aid course
EMT diploma or B.Sc. Nursing, BLS/AED, 2 yrs
Safety officer certificate and 1 year's service
Any first aid certificate, 6 months' service
source: Cl. 2.5: 2-yr EMT diploma or B.Sc (Nursing); AHA BLS with AED current certification; minimum 2 years' experience.

q: Which first aid treatments must be recorded in the First Aid Register?
source: Cl. 4.11: first aiders record all treatment (however minor) on the First Aid Register.

q: A first aider learns medical information about a casualty. Who may it be released to?
source: Cl. 4.11: keep confidential all information; medical information must only be released to relevant medical staff.

q: How long is the 'Train-the-Trainers' first aid programme organized by the HSE Induction Center?
source: Cl. 5.6.1: HSE Induction Center shall organize a 3-day 'Train-the-Trainers' programme.

q: Workers who handled paint or chemicals must do what before taking meals?
source: Cl. 5.1: persons handling chemicals, paint or toxic substances must thoroughly wash their hands before meals and before leaving site.

q: What must be done with an eye wash bottle once it has been opened?
options: Close it and keep it for next use
Keep it in the kit for one month
Dispose of it and replace it
source: Cl. 5.12: eye wash bottles once opened should be disposed of and replenished.

q: Who initiates the First Aid Needs Assessment?
source: Cl. 4.6 / 5.3: the concerned Group HSE Officer / HSE Coordinator / nominee shall initiate the First Aid Need Assessment.

q: Cardio Pulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) combines which two actions?
options: Cooling the body and giving oral fluids
source: Cl. 2.4: CPR combines rescue breathing and chest compressions.

q: Where is a Contractor Medic required to staff a First Aid Room?
options: At rig camps and remote locations
source: Cl. 5.5 II E: Contractor Medic is required in First Aid Rooms at rig camps and remote locations.

q: In an open yard storage area, what is the maximum height to which combustible materials may be piled?
source: Cl. 5.2.1: combustible materials shall in no case be piled higher than 20 ft (6.1 m).

q: What minimum width must driveways between and around combustible storage piles be kept?
source: Cl. 5.2.1: driveways between and around combustible storage piles must be at least 15 ft (4.57 m) wide.

q: Under KOC.GE.034, combustible material may NOT be stored outdoors within what distance of a building or structure?
source: Cl. 5.2.1: no combustible material may be stored outdoors within 10 ft (3.048 m) of a building or structure.

q: In an indoor store with sprinklers, what minimum clearance must be kept between the top of stored material and the sprinkler deflectors?
source: Cl. 5.2.2: clearance of at least 36 inches (0.9144 m) must be maintained between stored material and sprinkler deflectors.

q: Non-compatible materials that may create a fire, explosion or reaction hazard must be segregated in storage by a barrier with a fire resistance of at least:
source: Cl. 5.2.2: non-compatible materials must be segregated by a barrier having a fire resistance of at least 1 hour.

q: Where needed for access to doors, windows or standpipe connections, aisles must be kept at least how wide?
source: Cl. 5.3: keep aisles at least 3 ft (0.9144 m) wide where necessary for access to doors, windows or standpipe connections.

q: What does KOC.GE.034 recommend regarding end-of-day cleaning on construction sites?
options: Cleaning is done by a separate night crew only
Work stops half an hour early for site cleaning
Housekeeping is done once a week on rest day
Cleaning is needed only before HSE inspections
source: Cl. 5.0 Note: it is highly recommended that construction activities cease half an hour before and that time be used for area cleaning / housekeeping.

q: Under KOC.GE.034, what must Team Leaders ensure regarding gasoline within the battery limits of KOC projects, facilities and drilling sites?
options: Gasoline may be stored in approved jerry cans up to 20 litres
No gasoline storage or refuelling is allowed
Gasoline may be stored if kept 15 m from buildings
Gasoline refuelling is allowed only during daylight
source: Cl. 4.1: ensure that no gasoline storage or its refuelling is allowed in the KOC jurisdiction battery limit of any projects / facilities / drilling sites.

q: Which phrase sums up housekeeping in KOC.GE.034?
options: A place for everything, everything in its place
Clean up only before HSE inspections
Store all materials close to the work face
Remove site waste once a month
source: Cl. 1.0 / 5.2: 'Housekeeping is about a place for everything and everything in its place'.

q: When must crude oil, chemical or diesel spills be cleaned up?
options: At the end of the shift
source: Cl. 5.1: crude oil / chemical / diesel spills shall be cleaned immediately; contaminated soil disposed per KOC.EV.007 / EV.008.

q: May electrical rooms or computer server rooms be used to store materials?
options: Yes, if proper shelves are fitted
Yes, but only for spare parts
No, not for materials of any kind
source: Cl. 5.2.2: electric rooms and computer server rooms are not to be used as storage rooms for materials of any kind.

q: What minimum distance must stored material be kept from a fire door opening?
source: Cl. 5.2.2: material must not be stored within 36 inches (0.9144 m) of a fire door opening.

q: Lumber that will be handled manually shall not be stacked higher than:
source: Cl. 5.2.2: lumber piles shall not exceed 20 ft; lumber handled manually shall not be stacked more than 16 ft (4.876 m).

q: What clearance must be kept around the path of travel of a fire door, unless a barricade is provided?
source: Cl. 5.2.2: a clearance of 24 inches must be maintained around the path of travel of fire doors unless a barricade is provided.

q: How should protruding reinforcement bars (rebars) on site be protected?
options: Left as they are, with a sign
source: Cl. 5.1: protruding rebars are to be provided with rebar caps to avoid personal injury.

q: Where must food and beverages NOT be stored?
source: Cl. 5.1: no food or beverages shall be stored in toilet rooms or in an area exposed to toxic materials.

q: Driveways between combustible storage piles must be spaced to give a maximum grid unit of:
source: Cl. 5.2.1: driveways must be so spaced that a maximum grid system unit of 50 ft by 150 ft is produced.

q: Who is responsible for good housekeeping in their own work area?
source: Cl. 4.3 / 5.0: employees are responsible for good housekeeping in their respective work areas; housekeeping is everyone's responsibility.

q: Inside a building under construction, material shall not be placed within what distance of a hoistway or floor opening?
source: Cl. 5.2.2: material shall not be placed within 6 feet of any hoistway or inside floor openings.

q: After a dust storm, how should dusty floors inside buildings be cleaned?
options: Wait for the next weekly cleaning
Blow it away with compressed air
Hose it down with plenty of water
source: Cl. 5.5: dusty floors cleaned as soon as possible after dust storms; vacuuming or soft-bristle sweeping to minimize airborne dust.

q: A worker's personal H2S monitor goes into alarm near a sour wellhead. What is the correct immediate response under KOC.GE.036?
options: Run downwind to the nearest vehicle and drive off
Don escape set, check windsock, walk crosswind
Stay in place and wait for Control Room instructions
Help colleagues nearer the release before leaving
source: Cl. 5.x Escape from H2S Release: put on escape-only respirator, observe windsock, walk (don't run) crosswind to Control Room / muster point; do not attempt to rescue others.

q: When purchasing personal H2S monitors, KOC.GE.036 recommends two alarm set points. What are they?
options: First alarm at or below 5 ppm; second at or below 10 ppm
First alarm at or below 10 ppm; second at or below 15 ppm
First alarm at or below 15 ppm; second at or below 50 ppm
First alarm at or below 20 ppm; second at or below 100 ppm
source: Cl. 5.3 c): units should alarm at or below 10 ppm (TWA/8 hrs) for the first alarm and at or below 15 ppm (STEL/15 min) for the second.

q: According to KOC.GE.036 Table 2, when H2S is between 10 and 15 ppm, work without respiratory protection is permitted for:
options: 15 min, up to 4 times per shift
30 min, up to 2 times per shift
source: Table 2: between 10 to 15 ppm, work is permitted for a 15-minute period without RPE, up to 4 times during an 8-hour shift.

q: Gas testing shows 60 ppm H2S at a worksite and the source cannot be isolated, purged or ventilated. Under KOC.GE.036, what is required for work to proceed?
options: No work is allowed above 50 ppm
source: Table 2: up to 100 ppm, work is permitted with positive-pressure supplied air respirator or 30-min SCBA only if the source cannot be isolated; above 100 ppm entry only for rescue.

q: Where should a personal H2S monitor be worn?
options: Inside the coverall pocket, away from dust
On the belt at waist level
source: Cl. 5.3 c): worn outside clothing close to the head, as this is where H2S will be ingested; shoulder or breast pocket is optimal.

q: A crew of 14 workers will carry out maintenance in an area where H2S hazards may be present, but the facility itself is not sour. What gas detection does KOC.GE.036 require?
options: One personal gas monitor for the crew
No detector, as the facility is not sour
One personal monitor per five workers
source: Cl. 4 Field Workers c): one personal monitor per crew below 10 workers; more than 10 workers — a tripod-mounted portable multi-gas detector; sour facility — every worker carries one.

q: KOC.GE.036 defines 'sour' hydrocarbons as oil or gas containing H2S above:
source: Cl. 2.0: sour hydrocarbons contain more than 0.001%, i.e. 10 ppm of hydrogen sulphide.

q: Why can opening a vessel that handled sour product be hazardous even after it has been drained?
options: Dry pyrophoric iron sulphide can self-ignite in air
H2S turns lighter than air once the vessel is open
Rust deposits stop portable gas detectors working
Sulphur dioxide is released when water is added
source: Cl. 5.2 f): pyrophoric scale (ferrous sulphide) reacts exothermically with oxygen and, when dry, auto-ignites at ambient temperature.

q: How often must personnel who may enter H2S hazardous areas receive H2S awareness training under KOC.GE.036?
source: Cl. 5.4 a): personnel who may be required to enter H2S hazardous areas shall receive annual H2S awareness.

q: Which description of hydrogen sulphide (H2S) is correct?
options: Colourless, heavier than air, rotten-egg smell
Colourless, lighter than air, garlic smell
Brown, heavier than air, no smell at all
Yellow, lighter than air, no smell at all
source: Cl. 2.0: H2S is a colourless, very toxic, corrosive, heavier than air, flammable gas with a strong odour of rotten eggs.

q: Why must workers NOT rely on smell to detect H2S?
options: Its smell can only be noticed indoors
It smells exactly the same as diesel
It has no smell at any concentration
It deadens the sense of smell quickly
source: Table 2 (IDLH): H2S deadens sense of smell in 3 to 15 minutes.

q: How must the facility sour gas alarm signal differ from the normal siren?
options: The same tone as the fire alarm
A silent signal, using lights only
source: Cl. 5.3 b): the sour gas alarm signal shall be different from the normal siren and easily recognisable.

q: Work is planned 700 m from a sour gas facility. What does KOC.GE.036 require regarding windsocks?
options: Windsocks only if work exceeds 8 hours a day
None, as the work is outside the facility fence
A single windsock at the facility's main gate
source: Cl. 5.4 c): all facilities and work within 1 km of sour gas facilities shall have windsocks indicating which way to escape.

q: How many escape routes and assembly points should the JSA consider for work in an H2S area?
options: At least two routes, one assembly point
One route, at least two assembly points
source: Cl. 5.4 d): escape routes (at least two) and assembly points (at least two), depending on the location of the potential incident.

q: A colleague collapses near a sour wellhead. Under KOC.GE.036, what must you NOT do?
options: Move crosswind to the muster point
source: Cl. 4.9 h) / 5.5 c): workers shall not attempt rescue without SCBA; personnel shall not rescue others without first protecting themselves.

q: What respiratory protection must a trained rescuer wear when attempting rescue in an H2S release?
source: Cl. 5.5 c): positive-pressure, 30-minute SCBA shall always be worn when attempting rescue, with a standby person.

q: An H2S-exposed worker has red, painful eyes. How long should the eyes be flushed with clean water?
source: Cl. 5.5 d): if the victim's eyes are red and painful, flush with large amounts of clean water for at least 15 minutes.

q: Under the Ministry of Oil Regulations quoted in KOC.GE.036, how must work in a sour crude or sour gas environment be staffed?
options: With a supervisor visiting every hour
Alone, if he is carrying a radio
Alone, if wearing a personal H2S monitor
source: Cl. 3.1: no person shall work in a sour crude oil or sour gas environment without the continuous attendance of another person.

q: What minimum measuring range must a personal H2S monitor have?
source: Cl. 5.3 c): the measuring range shall cover at least 0 to 100 ppm with continuous read-out.

q: How often must the Asset / Directorate HSE Team carry out the H2S Hazard Management inspection of detection systems and RPE?
source: Cl. 4.7 d): carry out biannual 'HSE Inspection' using the H2S Hazard Management Inspection Checklist (Appendix 6).

q: Where must muster points be available around a work location in an H2S area?
options: Only at the main facility gate
On both sides (90°) of the work
Only downwind of the work area
source: Cl. 4.5 g): ensure that muster points are available on both sides (90 degree) of the work location.

q: The permanent place of safety in a Sour Gas Release Contingency Plan must always remain below what H2S level?
source: Cl. 5.5 a) x: a permanent place of safety shall always remain below 10 ppm (8 Hour TWA).

q: What is the minimum isolation standard required for entry into a vessel or confined space under KOC.PS.016?
options: Single block valve, locked and tagged
Double block and bleed valve isolation
ESD valve closed with actuator enabled
source: Cl. 5.1 / 5.5.1: the minimum isolation standard for vessel or confined space entry is positive isolation; it is mandatory for such entry.

q: Which is the PREFERRED method of achieving positive isolation according to KOC.PS.016?
options: Closing two block valves with an open bleed
Spool removal with rated blank flanges on the live ends
Inserting a spade only when spool removal is easier
Closing a single gate valve and locking it
source: Cl. 5.5.1: spool removal is the preferred method of positive isolation; spade insertion where spool removal is not reasonably practicable; valves alone are not positive isolation.

q: Before breaking containment, how long does KOC.PS.016 recommend that isolation integrity tests be conducted, as a minimum?
source: Cl. 5.7: all isolations shall be tested and shown to be effective before containment is broken; integrity tests recommended for a minimum of 10 minutes.

q: What is the minimum recommended frequency for monitoring the integrity of isolation points while containment is broken?
options: Once per week, at the start of the work week
Once per day, at the start of day shift only
Once per shift and just before breaking containment
Only when the Work Party requests a check
source: Cl. 5.8: minimum recommended monitoring frequency is once per shift and immediately prior to breaking containment; results recorded at shift handover.

q: Which type of valve shall NOT be used as a form of isolation under KOC.PS.016?
options: Fail-closed ESD valve with actuator disabled
source: Cl. 5.9: non-return (check) valves, flow control valves and pressure relief valves shall not be used as a form of isolation.

q: During work under a double block and bleed isolation, the gauge on the bleed between the two block valves starts to show pressure. What must happen?
options: Open the bleed fully and continue working
Stop work and review and amend the isolation
Tighten the upstream valve and continue
Record it at shift handover and continue
source: Cl. 5.5.2: the void between block valves must remain at 0 barg; if pressure increases, work shall stop and the isolation be reviewed and amended.

q: Besides vessel entry, KOC.PS.016 recommends positive isolation for long-duration isolations. What duration is given as an example?
source: Cl. 5.5.1: positive isolation recommended for long duration isolations, e.g. more than one week, hot work, and new/out-of-service equipment interfaces.

q: Under KOC.PS.016, how are bleeds and vents that form part of an isolation to be controlled?
options: Padlocked shut like the block valves
Left untagged so they can be operated
Tagged and recorded, without a lock
Removed from the line and blanked
source: Cl. 5.13: bleeds and vents do not require a securing device, as their position may change, but they require a bleed/vent tag and must be documented on the Certificate.

q: Which of the following is a form of positive isolation?
options: A closed and locked gate valve
source: Cl. 2.0 / 5.5.1: positive isolation is physical separation, e.g. blinding, spading, spool removal or air gapping.

q: Why is valve isolation alone NOT regarded as positive isolation?
options: Valves are too slow to close
source: Cl. 5.5.1: valve isolation alone is not sufficient to be classified as positive isolation because of the potential for valves to leak.

q: Who prepares the Mechanical Isolation Certificate?
source: Cl. 4.3 / 5.4: the Authorised Isolator plans and prepares the isolation by completing the Mechanical Isolation Certificate.

q: Who is ultimately responsible for ensuring the installed isolation is correct and authorizing the isolation work to proceed?
source: Cl. 4.2: the PRA is ultimately responsible for ensuring the isolation is correct and for authorizing the isolation work.

q: What right does the Work Party (Performing Authority) have regarding an isolation?
options: To remove locks during break time
To ask for proof of isolation integrity
source: Cl. 4.4: the Performing Authority has the right to request demonstration of the integrity of any isolation.

q: When may pressure, vacuum or thermal relief valves be isolated during an isolation?
options: Only after full isolation with vents open
First, before any other valve is closed
Whenever the Work Party requests it
source: Cl. 5.4 Note 3: do not isolate relief valves until the equipment is fully isolated and adequate vents are open.

q: An electrically operated valve is used as an isolation point. What is required?
options: A tag on the valve only
Nothing extra if it is closed
source: Cl. 5.6.2: electrically operated valves shall have their power supply positively isolated and locked.

q: Pneumatically operated valves that FAIL OPEN should normally:
options: Be used with air supply connected
source: Cl. 5.6.2: pneumatically and hydraulically operated valves which fail open should not normally be used for isolation purposes.

q: What material must isolation tags be made of?
source: Cl. 5.14: all tags must be made of plastic or other weatherproofing material and secured against accidental removal.

q: An isolation valve cannot be locked and could be opened by accidental contact. What should be done?
options: Paint the valve handle bright red
Tie the handle with plastic tape
Leave it and fit a second tag
source: Cl. 5.6.2: when isolating any valve that cannot be locked, the valve handle shall be removed where practicable.

q: Under what condition may an ESD valve be used for isolation?
options: Fail-open, with air supply left on
Used only as a bleed valve
source: Cl. 5.9: ESD valves may be used for isolation provided they are fail closed and the actuator is disabled.

q: An isolation valve is found to be passing slightly. What must be done before deciding whether work can proceed?
options: Tell HSE Group after the job
Proceed, as the leak is small
source: Cl. 5.9.1: whenever an isolation is compromised by passing valves, a risk assessment must be made of each isolation point.
